First, I ruled out a full rewrite — cleaner, but far too risky for the runway — and made a targeted change to the Scala and Spark pipeline so the blast radius stayed small. That pipeline processes millions of records daily, so one wrong rule misstates a large volume. The trade-off cost real technical debt: I left [the duplicated rule-mapping logic] in place, logged it as [a tracked remediation ticket], and scheduled the rewrite for [the next quarterly release]. Second, [the compliance stakeholder] wanted me to hold for the usual review cycle, which would've blown the date. Rather than just escalate, I walked them line by line through which rules the change touched and showed a reconciliation against [the prior period's known-good figures] — [about 40 rule mappings, all matching to the cent]. That evidence changed their mind on sequencing without us cutting controls, and we stayed on good terms because I brought data, not an opinion. Third, I built that reconciliation into the run so [the regulator-facing team] could verify independently. We submitted on time, inside a 100% compliance and zero-audit-failure track record across APAC. What I learned is that under pressure, narrowing scope and booking the debt so it actually gets paid is what saves you — I apply that same caution in my validation agent, which returns structured feedback rather than guessing when it can't confidently check something.

Describe how you handled competing prior.answer: I handle competing priorities by ranking on impact times urgency, agreeing that order in writing with my manager, and protecting whoever's blocked right now. At JPMorgan I owned two things on the Software Factory platform at once: a validation agent that checks whether generated code meets a Jira ticket's acceptance criteria, and the multi-service integration validation that confirms generated microservices interoperate end to end and triggers restarts on failure. Both feed the COB report workflow, so I couldn't just pick my favourite. First I made the trade-off visible: I listed what each piece unblocked and for whom, then took it to my manager so we agreed the order together. The deciding constraint was blast radius. Integration validation sat directly in the COB critical path, so a gap there could stall report generation for the whole downstream team, whereas the agent's feedback could improve incrementally. So I stabilised integration validation first, after [it caught two generated services disagreeing on a report number]. But the real pain wasn't mine — the downstream engineers were stuck decoding mismatches. I showed my manager a couple of their tickets so he could see the cost, then proposed owning the fix: a frontend agent surfacing root-cause analysis and remediation steps, so they could resolve mismatches independently rather than waiting on me. He agreed, and those engineers shaped what 'actionable' meant. Across that combined workflow we cut manual developer intervention by 90% and sped COB report generation by 70%. What I learned is the expensive mistake isn't choosing wrong, it's choosing silently. I applied that straight after on the APAC regulatory reporting, writing priorities down and confirming them with compliance stakeholders upfront.

Describe a time you changed your mind ab.answer: I changed my mind about rebuilding a pipeline wholesale versus profiling first, and it reshaped how I approach every performance problem now. At Blue Yonder, our data construction took about 10 days, and volume was growing towards 80M+ records a month. I was responsible for getting that down to something usable for the downstream teams who were blocked waiting on it. My first instinct was to rewrite the whole thing end to end in a streaming model straight away. I started down that path, but a senior teammate pushed back — his concern was that [a full rewrite risked correctness regressions nobody could verify against the old output]. I'll admit I initially resisted, because the rewrite felt cleaner. So instead of arguing, I actually profiled the existing pipeline properly, and I was wrong about where the time went — the real bottleneck was [a sequential batch join that serialised everything], not the parts I'd assumed. That changed my mind completely. I redesigned around Kafka streaming and pushed heavy transforms into Snowflake, but I kept the old pipeline running in parallel and compared outputs record by record before cutting over, and I rolled it out in stages. We got it from 10 days to under 8 hours, over 95% faster, and the teams waiting on that data were unblocked. The lesson was simple but it stuck: measure before you redesign, and treat a colleague's doubt as a signal, not an obstacle. I applied it directly at JPMorgan — before touching the COB reporting flow, I profiled and mapped the manual steps first, which is why we got to 90% less manual intervention without breaking anything.

Describe a time you measured the impact.answer: The clearest example is the pipeline rebuild I led at Blue Yonder, where measuring the impact changed both what we shipped and who I brought along. I weighed two options: just parallelising the existing full rebuilds, or moving to incremental loads with Kafka streaming. Parallelising was the right call if volumes had been flat and I'd needed a quick win without touching correctness — but with volume climbing towards 80 million a month, full rebuilds wouldn't scale, so I chose incremental loads despite the upfront complexity. I validated correctness row-for-row against the old pipeline before anyone relied on it. The build dropped from ten days to under eight hours, over ninety-five percent faster, so those reporting teams got same-day data instead of waiting a week, and it fed into the 600-plus engineering hours we saved annually. The lasting lesson was that the baseline tells you the truth — my assumption was wrong. I carried that straight into the Sigma BI overhaul: I measured query-and-display time first, found it was three minutes, and that number drove the redesign down to under forty seconds.

Tell me about a time you simplified a pr.answer: I'll lead with the headline: at Blue Yonder I spotted a chunk of repetitive manual operational work that nobody owned, automated it away, and saved over 600 engineering hours a year — and because the datasets I was refreshing fed the pipelines two of our flagship products depended on, the reliability win landed well beyond my own team. The situation was that every cycle our team ran a set of recurring operational steps by hand — [reconciling and refreshing datasets through a series of manual Snowflake queries]. It wasn't on anyone's roadmap; it was just the tax everyone paid, and it was eating into time we owed the product our customers cared about. It wasn't formally my job, but I kept getting pulled in, so I took ownership. First I mapped out every manual step and timed where the pain actually was, rather than guessing. Then I rebuilt the whole flow as Snowflake stored procedures so it ran on a schedule with no human in the loop. I weighed just writing a runbook — far cheaper to build and maintain, no procedures to version or debug — but a runbook still burns a person every cycle, and people's time was the binding constraint, so I automated. If the logic had been changing weekly, I'd have chosen the runbook, because maintaining brittle procedures against a moving target costs more than it saves. I validated it by running automated output alongside the manual process for [two cycles] and diffing results before switching people off. The result was 600-plus hours a year given back, and reliable downstream data. What I learned is to hunt for invisible recurring work — I applied that later at JPMorgan, cutting manual developer intervention by 90%.

Tell me about a time you had to deliver.answer: I delivered a new APAC regulatory report under a regulator-set filing deadline that couldn't move, and hit 100% compliance with zero audit failures. What is the most useful feedback you hav.answer: The most useful feedback I've ever had came from a senior engineer at Blue Yonder, in a code review. He told me I was optimising before I'd measured anything. I'd been reworking a data pipeline and jumped straight to parallelising a step I was sure was slow, with no profiling to back it up. My first instinct was to defend myself, but he'd framed it as a question about the data, not an attack, so I went and actually profiled it. The real cost was somewhere I hadn't suspected — [the batch join was single-threaded] — so I reworked my approach around the numbers instead of my gut. Where it really paid off was the big rebuild. The ten-day data-construction job wasn't on anyone's roadmap as a problem yet, but I could see it wouldn't survive the growth to 80M-plus records a month, so I proposed owning the overhaul myself and took it end to end. This time I profiled first. The choice was more parallelism on the Python ETL — quick to build but it kept fragile state in the app layer and wouldn't scale — versus Kafka streaming with transforms pushed into Snowflake, which cost more upfront but scaled with the warehouse. I chose the streaming route, validated the new output against the old, and rolled it out in stages. We got it from ten days to under eight hours, over 95% faster, and every downstream team that waited on that data got it the same day. The lesson stuck two ways: I lead with evidence now, and in my own reviews I ask people to show me profiling or test numbers — about the work, not the person.

Where do you think you are weakest, and.answer: My weakest area has been knowing when to stop refining and ship. Early on at Blue Yonder I'd polish a pipeline or a query well past the point where it changed anything for users, and a senior colleague told me straight: I was optimising for elegance while customers waited three minutes per Sigma query. That stung, but they were right, so I asked them to show me a specific case, and once I saw it I couldn't argue. I changed my approach on the spot. I now anchor every piece of work to a user outcome and a crisp definition of done, and I timebox the first version. On the Sigma overhaul I set the target explicitly and got query-and-display time from three minutes to under forty seconds across both flagship products, shipping in stages rather than chasing perfect. I carried that into JPMorgan: on the validation agent I built the smallest version covering the clear acceptance criteria and returning structured feedback when it couldn't decide, then iterated from real failures. That cut manual developer intervention by 90% and accelerated COB reports by 70%. But I didn't keep the lesson to myself — I wrote it up as a short 'ship-then-iterate' checklist and raised it in code review so the team anchors acceptance criteria and a definition of done before building. The one I'm still working on is estimating: I'm optimistic on the last ten percent, so I now pad explicitly for integration and review and flag risk early. The lesson that stuck: shipping something useful and iterating beats perfecting in private.

Tell me about a time you stepped outside.answer: The furthest I've stepped outside my comfort zone was taking on APAC regulatory reporting at JPMorgan. I'd spent my career in data pipelines and supply-chain systems, and suddenly a single wrong field could mean an audit failure in a jurisdiction whose rules I didn't yet know. The stakes were far higher than anything I'd handled, and that was genuinely uncomfortable. My brief was the reports themselves, but I realised the real risk sat upstream: the regulatory requirements weren't written as anything a system could test, so I took on translating them, which wasn't strictly my remit. Rather than fake confidence, I sat with [the compliance analyst] to turn each requirement into a concrete, testable rule. One around [reportable transaction thresholds] was ambiguous, so I wrote my assumptions down and got them confirmed before writing a line of logic. Then I had a choice: write every requirement as an explicit rule, which was thorough but slow, or move fast and spot-check. A teammate pushed back that full rigour was slowing delivery. I agreed the cost was real, so I showed them the audit exposure on the high-risk reportable fields versus the rest, and we agreed to tier it — full rigour on high-risk, faster elsewhere. That changed their mind, and the tiered approach became the team's standard. We went from [roughly three audit findings a quarter on the legacy reports] to 100% compliance and zero audit failures across those jurisdictions, on volumes of [tens of millions of records a month]. What I learned is the way out of discomfort isn't faking confidence, it's making the unknown explicit. I applied that directly on the validation agent I now own: it returns structured feedback when something can't be checked, rather than guessing.

Describe a time feedback changed how you.answer: The feedback that changed how I work came early at Blue Yonder, during the pipeline rebuild that took data construction from 10 days to under 8 hours. I was proud of the performance gain, but in review a senior engineer told me plainly that I'd optimised for speed and skipped the data-quality checks, so if the output were wrong, nobody would catch it until a customer did. That stung, because I'd led with the numbers. But he was right. My habit until then was to prove a thing was fast, then add validation later. So I changed the order. I added [row-count and checksum reconciliation between old and new output] before I rolled anything out, and I made the comparison against the legacy pipeline a gate, not an afterthought. It caught [a mismatch on one join] that I'd have shipped. More importantly, I carried that lesson forward. When I later built the Snowflake automation that saved 600+ hours a year, I designed the correctness checks first and the performance second, and when I moved to JPMorgan I architected a validation agent whose whole job is to check generated code against acceptance criteria before it's trusted — correctness as a gate is now the spine of how I work, and it supports zero audit failures on APAC reporting. The lesson I took wasn't just 'add tests'. It was that I should be as proud of proving something is correct as I am of proving it's fast, and I should invite the hard review early, while it's cheap to change course.

Tell me about a time you asked for help.answer: I'll pick the time I rebuilt our data pipeline at Blue Yonder, because I only cracked it after asking for help — and that meant bringing a sceptical reviewer round too. We were constructing a dataset that took about 10 days, with volume growing towards 80M+ records a month, so the whole reporting flow was at risk, and I owned getting that construction time down. I profiled it, found [the batch join was single-threaded], and spent a couple of days trying to parallelise it myself. It wasn't fast enough, so rather than keep grinding I asked [a senior data engineer] to review my approach. That was hard, because I'd wanted to own it end to end. He suggested pushing the heavy transforms down into Snowflake instead of moving data out to transform it. Initially he wanted a full rebuild straight away; I pushed back because I was worried about the extra Snowflake compute cost on 80M records a month. So I ran a small benchmark on one month's data — it showed the push-down plus incremental Kafka loads was both faster and cheaper per run, since we stopped shuttling data around. That evidence changed his mind on sequencing, and it changed mine on the approach. I rebuilt it, validated correctness row by row against the old output, and rolled it out in stages. Construction time went from 10 days to under 8 hours, over 95% faster, which unblocked every team depending on those reports. What I learned is that asking for help early is a strength — and the best way to settle a design disagreement is a cheap experiment, not opinion. Later at JPMorgan, when acceptance criteria were ambiguous, I went straight to the ticket authors rather than guessing.

Tell me about a skill you deliberately b.answer: The skill I deliberately built this past year is making non-deterministic AI output trustworthy in a regulated setting, and knowing when verification is worth its cost. When I took ownership of a validation agent inside JPMorgan's Software Factory, I knew distributed pipelines, but I'd never built anything where the core engine could be confidently wrong. So I set a rule: generated code stays untrusted until it's checked against the ticket's acceptance criteria. I practised by building the smallest version first, turning Jira criteria into concrete checks and returning structured feedback for self-correction rather than letting the model guess. Where it failed, [usually an ambiguous criterion the model over-interpreted], I'd study it and tighten the checks. The harder half was influence. Some senior engineers were genuinely sceptical about an LLM near regulated COB reporting, and they were right to be. So rather than argue, I asked what would convince them; the real concern was auditability. I ran the agent in shadow mode against [a batch of past tickets], showed where it caught mismatches a human had missed, and agreed it would only ever flag, never silently pass, on anything ambiguous. That changed their minds with evidence, and their push for an audit trail is now a core feature. One engineer was right that flagging everything would hurt throughput, so I added confidence tiers rather than block the pipeline. Starting from an almost entirely manual workflow, I got manual developer intervention down 90% and COB generation 70% faster, with zero audit failures, and the whole reporting team relies on it now. What I learned is the skill isn't 'using AI', it's building guardrails and verifying hardest where the cost of being wrong is an audit failure.

When I joined JPMorgan I had to get up to speed on Scala and Apache Spark fast, because the APAC regulatory reporting I owned ran entirely on that stack and filing dates don't move. Those reports don't just serve my team — they go to [APAC regulators and the firm's audit function], so a late or wrong filing is a firm-level compliance problem, not a local one. My background was Python and Kafka, so I owed it to those downstream consumers not to become the bottleneck. I didn't try to read everything — I rebuilt one small, non-critical report end to end, validating my output against [the prior quarter's filed figures] until they matched exactly. A senior engineer pushed back: he felt I should learn the whole codebase before touching anything, to avoid naive mistakes. He was partly right — I did write Scala in a Python mindset early and [over-collected a dataset to the driver]. But I showed him the validated rebuild and the Scala gotchas note I'd started, and argued a correct sandboxed build taught the patterns faster and more safely. He agreed to try it. Rather than leave that note informal, I proposed folding it into the team's onboarding material with a named owner, so it outlives any one person — the next two joiners ramped off it without repeating my dead ends. I delivered the APAC reports with 100% compliance and zero audit failures through a risky handover. What I learned is that under a hard deadline, building one real thing correctly beats reading everything — I used the same approach later for Snowflake query optimisation. But for genuinely novel or security-sensitive code, where there's no baseline to validate against, I'd invest in reading and design review first.

Describe something you believed strongly.answer: I used to believe you simply couldn't let an LLM anywhere near the critical path in a regulated domain like financial reporting — a subtly wrong output was never worth the speed, so I'd push for deterministic automation every time. What changed my mind was the COB report work at JPMorgan. When I proposed letting LLMs and AI agents into the Close of Business workflow, I was a sceptic myself, and so was [a senior compliance engineer] who worried a wrong report could trigger an audit finding. So instead of arguing from opinion, I ran a small, contained experiment. I kept the LLM out of the actual regulatory logic and used it only to draft work that was then checked — every output had to pass acceptance-criteria validation, tests and integration checks before it went near a report. I compared the agent's results against known-good historical outputs on [a bounded set of past COB runs]. The evidence was hard to ignore: manual developer intervention down 90%, COB generation 70% faster, 100% compliance and zero audit failures. Crucially, I didn't leave it in my own pipeline. I wrote up the verification pattern, and the APAC reporting teams adopted the same checks-first approach for their generated microservices — on [their first adopted service] they went from [about two days of manual review per run] to review only on failed checks, with [zero audit findings since]. I was wrong that AI couldn't be trusted in a regulated setting; I was right it couldn't be trusted blindly. The answer was verification, not avoidance. Now my default is that generated code is untrusted until checked, and I design the checks first — that principle is exactly what I built my validation agent around.

Why Google, and why now?.answer: The short version: Google's where my last five years converge, and the timing's right because I've just proven I can ship AI agents engineers trust in a regulated setting. My path's gone from co-founding Al-Shala and building an MVP for 1,000-plus concurrent users, to large-scale pipelines at Blue Yonder, where I cut dataset construction from 10 days to under 8 hours at 80M-plus records a month, to architecting and owning a validation agent at JPMorgan that checks generated code against acceptance criteria. The thread is building reliable systems at scale, and nowhere matters more than Google: infrastructure and developer tooling at a reach I can't get elsewhere, and a culture serious about correctness and testing. There's a real trade-off behind leaving. At JPMorgan I proposed putting LLMs into the Close-of-Business reporting workflow, and [a senior reviewer on the regulatory side] pushed back, worried an automated step could risk our compliance record. Before shadow mode I'd weighed two other options: a rules-only validator with no LLM, which was safe but couldn't handle the ambiguous criteria; and gating every report behind full manual review, which kept safety but gave none of the speed. I chose shadow mode because it let me get evidence without touching production, and I asked them what would convince them first. The lesson, prove safety with evidence before scaling, I applied from day one on the validation agent, so dependent teams now get root-cause feedback automatically. When I joined, building the core dataset for [which product] took around ten days, volume was climbing towards 80 million records a month, and downstream reporting teams were stuck waiting. Nobody had owned a redesign, so I put my hand up and took it end to end. I profiled it first and found the bottleneck was [a full nightly rebuild instead of incremental loads]. I weighed keeping heavy transforms in the existing Python versus pushing them into Snowflake; I chose Snowflake because at 80 million records the compute scaled where our code didn't, and the deciding factor was finishing within a daily window rather than raw cost. What I learned, and now do by default, is measure before you redesign and build data-quality checks in from day one. That instinct carried straight into my validation agent, which exists to catch problems automatically before they reach anyone.

Why this Software Engineer role at Googl.answer: The short version: this role lets me keep doing what I'm best at — building reliable systems at scale — but for products billions of people depend on, and I'm ready for that step now. My path has one thread. I co-founded a startup, built an MVP on AWS for over a thousand concurrent users, then at Blue Yonder scaled streaming pipelines to 80 million-plus records a month and cut data construction from ten days to under eight hours. There I noticed nobody owned the manual Snowflake steps teams kept tripping over, so I took that on outside my remit and automated them, saving 600-plus engineering hours a year across the two products — that taught me the impact that comes from reaching beyond your own tickets. At JPMorgan I own a validation agent for production AI, which cut manual intervention by 90% and sped COB reports by 70%. Early on, [a senior reviewer] didn't trust letting an LLM into a zero-audit-failure workflow, and honestly he was right to push — I ran a small shadow experiment against real tickets before we shipped, and that evidence changed the call. On Google over staying or a specialised infrastructure shop: I weighed depth in finance against breadth of reach, and reach won — the hard reliability problems live where real users can't tolerate failure. I'd choose the opposite, staying in a narrow domain, only if the hardest problems I wanted to solve lived there and the user reach didn't — here they don't. The trade-off is leaving a domain I've grown to love. That's why it's Google, and why it's now.

Explain what you work on now to someone.answer: Right now I'm building the quality-control brain for a kind of factory that writes software. At JPMorgan, a system generates a lot of code automatically to produce the big financial reports we send to regulators, and I architect and own the part that checks that work before anyone trusts it. Picture a factory line where a machine stamps out parts all day — you still need an inspector who holds each part against the blueprint and says this one's good, this one's wrong, and here's exactly why. That inspector is software I build. It reads the requirements in a ticket, checks the generated code meets them, and sends back clear feedback so the work gets fixed automatically rather than a person chasing it. When I first proposed letting an agent into this flow, some senior reviewers were rightly nervous about automating anything regulatory, so I didn't argue; I built a small proof that showed exactly where it flagged problems and where it honestly said 'I can't verify this', and that won them over. But I didn't stop at my own piece. I saw engineers across the reporting team losing hours to report number mismatches, which wasn't strictly my ticket, so I went and built a frontend agent that hands them the root cause and the fix steps directly, so they unblock themselves. That's the part I'm proudest of — spotting other people's pain and owning the fix. Against a baseline where almost every mismatch needed a developer to step in, manual intervention is now down 90% and end-of-day reports come out 70% faster, with 100% compliance and zero audit failures. Simply put, I teach software to check other software's homework, so engineers spend their time on the genuinely hard problems.
